questions: Did the redness and swelling of your face begin suddenly?
Is the affected area itchy?
Is it painful or tender?
Do you have swelling of your lips, tongue, or throat or any difficulty breathing?
Have you recently received an injection, medication, or cosmetic treatment involving your face?
Has this facial redness and swelling been present for more than a few weeks?
Does it come and go in episodes?
Is it triggered or worsened by heat, sunlight, exercise, hot drinks, spicy foods, or alcohol?
Do you have persistent redness or visible small blood vessels on your cheeks or nose?
Do you have similar redness, swelling, or thickening on other parts of your body?
Have you had fever, night sweats, weight loss, or joint pains?
Was there a pre-existing brownish or darker patch or spot on your forehead before it was rubbed?
Did the swelling and redness appear specifically after the doctor rubbed or scratched that spot?
Does rubbing or scratching the spot cause it to become raised, swollen, or itchy?
Do you have similar spots elsewhere on your skin?
Do you experience episodes of flushing, faintness, rapid heartbeat, abdominal cramps, or diarrhea?
When the forehead is firmly stroked or scratched, does a raised red welt appear within a few minutes?
Does that raised red area fade back to normal within an hour?
Have you ever developed raised welts or hives after pressure, scratching, or rubbing elsewhere on your body?
Do you have recurrent episodes of hives or swelling without a clear cause?
Did the forehead swelling and redness first appear during this consultation, after the examiner repeatedly pressed or manipulated the area?
Is the swelling limited mainly to the forehead and upper eyelids?
Has the swelling persisted for more than 24 hours?
Has this happened after pressure or minor trauma on a previous occasion?
Have you had any recent infection, insect bite, or injury to the forehead?
Did the facial redness and swelling completely resolve within several hours without treatment?
Was the swelling confined to areas that had been repeatedly rubbed or pressed?
Have you recently started using any new facial cleanser, cream, sunscreen, hair product, or cosmetic?
Do you take an ACE inhibitor such as lisinopril, enalapril, or ramipril?
Has anyone in your family had recurrent unexplained swelling of the face, hands, feet, or abdomen?
Is the redness and swelling predominantly on one side of your face?
Does the affected skin feel noticeably warmer than the unaffected skin?
Did the swelling begin after a dental procedure, vaccination, or other medical procedure?
Do you have tooth pain, sinus pain, nasal congestion, or discharge?
Do you have swelling elsewhere now, such as your hands, feet, or abdomen?
orders: Perform diascopy of the forehead and cheeks by pressing a transparent glass slide against the red areas to determine whether the erythema blanches.
Perform a focused cranial-nerve and facial examination, including assessment of facial sensation, facial symmetry, and forehead movement.

Perform a standardized dermographism provocation test by stroking uninvolved forearm skin with a blunt instrument at moderate pressure and observing for a linear wheal and surrounding erythema for 10 minutes.
Perform a complete skin examination for wheals, angioedema, flushing, and mastocytosis-associated lesions, including Darier’s sign on any pigmented lesions.
Measure serum C4 and quantitative and functional C1-esterase inhibitor levels.
Measure serum tryptase during the facial swelling and again at baseline.
Obtain a complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, and C-reactive protein.
